implementation_notes: Ruby's document is a Hash - or, when a typed carrier helps, a Struct or a Data.define value object - and the stdlib JSON module is the codec: JSON.generate/hash.to_json writes it and JSON.parse(body) returns hashes and arrays that the receiver reads directly, which is why the classic message class is unnecessary for the common case. Data.define (Ruby 3.2) gives immutable, keyword-initialised documents with to_h and deconstruction, the closest local equivalent of a DTO, while dry-struct or a schema library adds validation where documents cross a trust boundary. String versus symbol keys and the treatment of Time are the two representation decisions to fix before documents start flowing.
code_sketch:
Shipment = Data.define(:version, :order_id, :lines)

wire = JSON.generate(version: doc.version, order_id: doc.order_id, lines: doc.lines)

begin
  got = JSON.parse(wire)                  # string keys, plain hashes
rescue JSON::ParserError => e
  dead_letter(wire, e.message); return    # invalid message path
end
case got
when Hash then handle(got['order_id'], got)   # receiver decides
else ignore(got)
end
pitfalls: JSON.parse with create_additions: true instantiates classes named inside the payload, so untrusted documents must be parsed without additions.
JSON.generate refuses NaN/Infinity unless allow_nan: true, and that option emits non-standard JSON other systems reject; Time is only a string if you convert it yourself.
Parsed keys are strings, so code written against symbol keys silently matches nothing; mixing key types in one document is a classic Ruby bug.
JSON is not a framed protocol, so several documents concatenated on one stream are a single parse error - each message needs its own frame.
